 Use tab to navigate through the menu items. City Haze Celebrates Independent Success With New Single ‘Like We Are’ Featuring Kyle Owens
 Jennifer Gurton 2 minutes ago 6 min read South Bronx and Brooklyn-based hip-hop artist, producer, and creative director City Haze  is preparing to release his latest single, “Like We Are,” featuring Kyle Owens, on November 20, 2026. Accompanied by a cinematic official music video, the release celebrates confidence, perseverance, and the satisfaction of finally seeing years of hard work pay off. 
 City Haze has been building his independent career since 2008, earning early recognition through the Online Hip-Hop Awards and receiving the #1 Contender Award at the 2010 Underground Music Awards. His journey has included coverage from publications like XXL, AllHipHop, and HipHopDX, establishing a foundation long before today's social media-driven music landscape. Now , he's bringing that experience into a new creative chapter. 
 Self-produced, mixed, and mastered by City Haze, “Like We Are” combines his confident delivery with a melodic hook performed by featured artist and co-songwriter Kyle Owens. The song captures that late-night feeling of accomplishment when the sacrifices, setbacks, and relentless work finally begin making sense. 
 What we appreciate about this release is the distinction between confidence and empty bragging. There's a difference between pretending you've made it and recognizing everything you've survived to reach your current position. 
 The single also follows City Haze's ambitious Four Worlds  visual project, featuring “Ric Flair,” “Cheese Mac,” “The Message,” and “Supafly.” Together, the independently produced cinematic releases have reportedly surpassed 100,000 Instagram views. 
 Beyond the recording, City Haze directed and produced the accompanying AI-assisted music video, demonstrating his interest in expanding what's possible for independent artists working without traditional industry infrastructure. 
 With “Like We Are,” City Haze isn't waiting for someone else to validate his progress. 
 We caught up with City Haze to discuss his independent journey, collaborating with Kyle Owens, and the creative vision behind his latest release. Check out our exclusive interview below. 
 “Like We Are” celebrates the moment when years of hard work finally begin paying off. You've been building your career independently since 2008, so what does success mean to you today compared to when you first entered the industry, and was there a particular moment that inspired this record? 
 Back then, success was validation. In 2008, I was the only unsigned artist nominated for “King of the Net” at the Online Hip-Hop Awards alongside Soulja Boy, Lil Wayne, 50 Cent, Diddy, and Plies. That told me the internet chose me, the people chose me, and my sound could compete without a deal. 
 Then winning #1 Contender at the Underground Music Awards in 2010 taught me the real lesson: ownership. 
 Today, success isn’t just a chart position. It’s owning my catalog, building Clover Hospitality Group + Clover Group Creatives, and still being able to drop music I believe in 15+ years later. Longevity isn’t about being hot for a summer; it’s about surviving the seasons. 
 “Like We Are” came from that present-tense, late-night grind energy. That feeling when you’re riding, tunnel vision, and everything else quiets down. I produced it myself because I wanted that specific mood: smooth, cinematic, but still grounded. 
 You've experienced several different eras of hip-hop, from the underground blog and mixtape culture of the late 2000s to today's social media-driven industry. What do you believe independent artists have gained through that evolution, and what important elements of hip-hop culture do you think have been lost along the way? 
 Gained: direct access and control. 
 In the blog era, if XXL, HipHopDX, AllHipHop, DJBooth, 2DopeBoyz, NahRight, etc. posted you, people actually went and listened. Now, streaming and social media mean I can go directly to the fans. I don’t need a blog to co-sign me; I can show you the visual, the story, the world myself. The tools have changed; now I’m doing cinematic visuals, building whole worlds around a song, but the identity is the same. 
 Lost: music-first discovery and patience. 
 The blog era was the last time it was really about the music  first. No algorithm, no 15-second clip. You had to have a real record. What I miss is that grind and gatekeeping-by-taste: grinding emails, sending records, building relationships with editors, learning how to make one record stretch across 10 blogs. As an independe nt, I had to be my own label, manager, and promo. That taught me how to move. What hasn’t changed for me: melodic, soulful, East Coast music, written from real life. 
 You wrote, produced, mixed, and mastered “Like We Are,” while Kyle Owens contributed the melodic hook and co-writing. How did that collaboration come together, and what did Kyle bring to the record that helped complete the vision you originally had in mind? 
 Me and Kyle have history, going back to earlier records together like “Tell Me What’s Good,” where Kyle “K.O.” Owens tied it together with that smooth hook. For “Like We Are,” arriving November 20, 2026, I built it as a fully self-contained record, co-writing, producing, mixing, and mastering it myself to lock in that specific late-night mood. 
 What Kyle brought was the soul that completes it: 
 “I can rap the reality, but when he sings that hook, it opens the record up emotionally. It makes you feel what I’m saying. That contrast — my verses and his voice — is what makes the concept hit. It’s not just a song; it’s a moment.” 
 That’s the vision: my verses carry the reality and tunnel vision; his hook carries the feeling. 
 Your Four Worlds  project introduced four distinct cinematic identities through “Ric Flair,” “Cheese Mac,” “The Message,” and “Supafly.” What inspired you to approach these releases as separate visual worlds, and how does the official video for “Like We Are” bring those creative ideas together? 
 What connects them is ME . My approach to consistency across all of it: the core stays the same- melodic, soulful, East Coast, honest- but you let the world change around it.  Four different worlds, one vision. I wrote and directed all four. 
 I am not one thing. I am  a lot of things. I’m the businessman, I’m the kid from the Bronx and Brooklyn, and I’m the dreamer. 
 “Ric Flair”:  Luxury, confidence, penthouse energy. Neon, the coyote, that larger-than-life flex. It’s the champ talking. 
 “Cheese Mac”:  Harlem noir, 1940s-50s, fedora, pinstripe, a night at the jazz club called The Cheese Mac. Smooth, storytelling, classic.   
 “The Message”:  The heart. A coming-of-age story, a young boy writing “ STAR DREAMS” in his notebook, turning that dream into a galaxy, rooftop ciphers, rain-slick bodega streets. That’s where I came from. 
 “Supafly”:  Sci-fi epic. Military plane skydives, ancient stone chambers, glowing green chips, holographic control rooms. That’s my expression of an astral experience. 
 The rollout itself was sequenced as a summer run: idea June 23, “Ric Flair” July 21, “Cheese Mac” July 29, “The Message” Aug 5, “Supafly” Aug 12. 
 “Like We Are” brings those ideas together by pulling the cinematic approach inward. Instead of jumping to another fantasy world, I put myself in that car at night, with the city behind me, looking right at the camera, like that frame at 01:38 in the music video; it feels cinematic, like a movie, not just a music video. It’s my same director’s mindset from Four Worlds, but now the world is the real late-night grind: hustler’s story told in real time, tunnel vision, everything else quiet. 
 You're exploring AI filmmaking while maintaining hands-on control over your music and creative direction. As these technologies become increasingly accessible, where do you believe the line should exist between using AI to expand an artist's imagination and allowing technology to replace the human creativity that makes music meaningful? 
 For me, AI is a director’s tool, not a replacement for the artist. 
 I created “Like We Are” late at night, pushing my imagination and AI filmmaking creative direction. With AI filmmaking, I can direct the whole world myself, be the writer, director, and Star all at once, and show exactly what I imagined late at night when I made it. 
 The line is where the human feeling starts: 
 1.   Feeling first, technology second.  My process starts with feeling. If the beat doesn’t make me feel something, I can’t write to it. AI can build the visual world, but it can’t supply that honest, lived feeling. 
 2.   Human story stays in control.  Storytelling is everything to me. I'm not just dropping songs; I'm building worlds. If you can see  the record, you’ll remember it longer. AI expands imagination; it doesn’t get to decide the story, the emotion, or the truth of it. 
 3.   Ownership stays human.  That goes back to my whole career lesson: build my own audience, own relationships, own catalog; nobody can take that from me. Using AI to expand what one independent artist can direct is in that same spirit. Letting it replace the writing, the voice, the lived experience, and the direction would cross the line, because then it’s no longer my  vision.
